title: Sort Array By Parity
description: Rearrange an array so all even elements come before odd elements, using an in-place two-pointer partition.

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums, rearrange it so that all even elements appear before all odd elements. Any arrangement satisfying this condition is accepted; this document uses one specific two-pointer algorithm and shows its exact deterministic output.

blocks.caption: Two pointers converge inward, swapping only when both are stuck on the wrong parity.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","nums[] (arbitrary order)"],["Output","Same elements, evens before odds, any valid relative order accepted"],["Constraint","In-place rearrangement is possible and preferred for O(1) extra space"]]}

blocks.text: Partitioning an array into two groups based on a boolean condition (even versus odd) from both ends inward is the classic two-pointer partition pattern, the same idea behind partitioning a Quicksort pivot or the Dutch National Flag problem.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: A left pointer looking for a value in the "wrong" group and a right pointer looking for a value in the other "wrong" group, swapping when both are stuck, is a reusable partition technique across many array rearrangement problems.

Picture a sorter standing at both ends of a row of numbered cards, working inward. The left hand skips over any card that is already even (it is already in the right place). The right hand skips over any card that is already odd (also already in place). When both hands are stuck on a card in the wrong group, they swap those two cards and both step one position inward.

blocks.caption: Both pointers skip correctly-placed values and swap only when both are stuck.

items: left advances past any already-even value; right retreats past any already-odd value.
A swap only happens when left points to an odd value AND right points to an even value, both simultaneously "stuck."
The process is done when left meets or passes right, at which point every even value is to the left of every odd value.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The final array is [4, 2, 1, 3]. Both evens (4, 2) appear before both odds (1, 3), satisfying the condition, and this is exactly the deterministic result of this specific two-pointer algorithm on this input.
A simple approach separates the array into two new lists, one for evens and one for odds, then concatenates them. This is correct and easy to reason about, but uses O(n) extra space.

Since the goal only cares about the RELATIVE grouping (not a specific order within each group), an in-place two-pointer partition achieves the same result using no extra array: converge from both ends, and swap only when a value is found on the wrong side.
Build two separate lists (evens and odds) in a single pass, then concatenate them.

codes.python:
def sort_array_by_parity(nums):
    evens = [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]
    odds = [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 1]
    return evens + odds


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(sort_array_by_parity([3, 1, 2, 4]))
    print(sort_array_by_parity([0]))

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: The extra O(n) space for the two new lists is unnecessary, since the array can be rearranged in place.

Use two pointers starting at both ends, converging inward. Advance left past already-even values, retreat right past already-odd values, and swap the two "stuck" values whenever left points to odd and right points to even, then move both pointers inward. This achieves the same grouping in place, with no extra array.

items: left moves right while arr[left] is even.
right moves left while arr[right] is odd.
When both are stuck (left is odd, right is even), swap them and advance both pointers.

items: Grouping elements by a boolean condition, without caring about order within each group, is solvable in-place with a two-pointer partition.
Advancing each pointer past already-correctly-placed values, and swapping only when both are stuck, is the general Dutch-flag-style partition pattern.
This technique reapplies to any "rearrange so all X come before all not-X" problem, regardless of what X represents.

blocks.text: Sort Array By Parity is solved with an in-place two-pointer partition: a left pointer skips already-even values, a right pointer skips already-odd values, and a swap resolves the two "stuck" positions when found, converging to a fully grouped array in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
